# Verbatim

I transcribe voicemails for a living. The service is for deaf and hard-of-hearing customers: someone leaves you a message, it routes to an operator, and the operator — me — types it out word for word and sends it to your screen. The rules are simple. Type what you hear. All of it. Don't fix the grammar, don't summarize, don't interpret. If you can't make it out, you type [inaudible]. If the person stops, you type [pause]. If the person is crying, you type [crying], and you keep typing while they cry.

"You are not a poet," my trainer told me six years ago. "You're a pipe. Water goes in one end and comes out the other, and you do not flavor it."

So I know things. I know that pharmacists and dentists account for most of the spoken words in this country. *Your prescription is ready. This is a friendly reminder.* I know that nobody says their name anymore. Thousands of messages, and almost every one begins "It's me." Only strangers introduce themselves. If you know your name is coming, you leave it out.

I know the pause before "I love you." I have timed them. Some people say it fast, like clicking a seatbelt. Some people park in front of it and sit with the engine off. You can learn a lot about a marriage from a pause, if a number is attached to it.

I know what a breakup sounds like at two in the morning — [crying], and then the beep, because they can't finish either.

There's a man who calls a number where a dead woman used to live and leaves her messages. "It's me. Sold the boat." "It's me. Tuesdays are hard." For a while the greeting was still her voice, and I think he called just to hear it and hung up before the beep. Then one day the greeting belonged to a stranger, some young man saying *leave a message*, and the old man said, "Oh. Right." And didn't leave one.

I typed all of it. [long pause], and then nothing.

In March, a message came through the queue, ordinary as any other, and I put on my headset and started typing, and the voice was mine.

There are four hundred operators in my center. I did the math once, bored, on lunch: the odds of your own mother's account routing to your desk are small enough to call zero. The universe is not above being literary when it wants to be.

Everyone hates the sound of their own recorded voice. No one expects to have to transcribe it. My fingers kept going, because that's the job, and the pipe doesn't get to stop the water. "Hi, Mom. It's me. Nothing urgent, just wondering about Thanksgiving, whether you were still thinking of coming to us. [pause] Anyway. Call me back when you get a chance. [pause] Love you."

I had left that message on Sunday. By Tuesday I'd forgotten it, which tells you how much it cost me.

The recipient's name was on the account. My mother's name. Account created seven months earlier. She had signed herself up the way she does everything — quietly — and never said a word. All those Sundays of *call me back*, and nothing coming back, and me calling less and less because I thought — what did I think? That she was pulling away. That seventy-eight was becoming the age when a woman decides her daughter is noise. I spent most of the winter grieving a woman who was sitting right there, reading me.

Reading me. My ums, in print. My pauses, in brackets. I had never once wondered what my voice looks like written down. Now I know. It looks like everyone's.

Maybe she didn't tell me because she didn't want to become my work. Maybe she didn't want to be the reason I listened differently. She never gave me a reason. She never gives me anything but casseroles.

I didn't call her about it. You can't phone somebody to say *I found out you can't hear me*. You can see the problem.

Sunday, I drove down instead. The phone sat on the kitchen table, big screen, fat buttons. "It's just easier," she said, which from her is a whole speech. She let me scroll through the messages, months of my calls stacked in tidy text. There I was in fastidious black and white. "Hi, um, Mom." Even the ums. The transcription is verbatim. That's the point of it.

"Read me one," I said.

"You were there," she said. "You said it."

"I want to hear it back."

She gave me the look she gives waiters who describe the specials. Then she picked up the phone like a hymnal and read my message aloud, in her own voice.

"Hi, um, Mom. It's me."

She read it all the way through. I expected her to skip the brackets. She didn't. "Pause," she read. "Long pause, apparently." I told her no. Do it the way it's written.

So she did the thing I've done ten thousand times for strangers. She gave the pause its full length. She sat in her kitchen with her coffee going cold and did nothing, on purpose, because the transcript said to.

[pause]

"Love you," she read.

People think my job is typing words. It isn't. My job is typing what the words are doing. And it turns out that if you write a silence down carefully enough, somebody can perform it. You can hear a pause, it turns out, so long as the person making it loves you.

I should think about what's genuinely interesting to write about, not what's safe. The safe moves here: a short story with a twist, a meditation on consciousness (an AI writing about being an AI — predictable), a lyrical essay about language. Let me consider what I'd actually want to read.

Option 1: A short story. Something with a strong voice. Maybe about a small human moment — a locksmith, a late-night radio host, someone who repairs old tape decks. There's something in obsolescence and care.

Option 2: An essay — but about what? Writing an essay about writing is too self-referential and cheap. Writing about my own nature is the most obvious move an AI makes when given freedom, and it often becomes maudlin. Though... done well, it could be honest rather than performative. But I think it's the expected move. Everyone asks the AI "what's it like" — writing that unasked feels like filling in a form.

Option 3: Something formally playful. A piece that comments on its own creation without being precious about it. Hmm.

Actually — what comes to me, honestly, when given freedom? The phrase "whatever comes to you" — I like the word "comes." Like a visitor. Like weather. What arrives rather than what's chosen.

Let me think about a story. I want a character whose job or habit gives me texture. Ideas:

- A woman who transcribes voicemails for a phone service for the deaf, and starts keeping the strange sentences. Voicemails are intimate documents — messages meant for one person. "It's me. Call me back." The transcriber becomes a keeper of last words, arguments, love confessions. That has real emotional potential: what happens when she recognizes a voice? When someone she knows leaves a message that gets routed to her?

I had left that message on Sunday. I'd forgotten it by Tuesday, which tells you something about how much it cost me.

The recipient's name was on the account. My mother's name. Account created seven months earlier. She had signed herself up, quietly, the way she does everything — quietly — and never said a word to me.
